verdicts.trueWording: owes much more to the richly populated Victorian novel
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'But Kay's work owes much more to the richly populated Victorian novel than to the sparser contemporary novel; in fact, its closest correlation is to the thick historical novel of the Dorothy Dunnett tradition.' The contrast class is Tolkien/Donaldson/Wolfe/Kinsella. Precision note for re-use: Randall's wording is 'the four fantasies mentioned above are focalized through one or two central characters' - not 'single-focalizer'. Do not re-quote him as saying single.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "single-focalizer" applied to Tolkien/Donaldson/Wolfe — the note says Randall's wording is "focalized through one or two central characters" and instructs "Do not re-quote him as saying single".

verdicts.trueWording: Kay seems determined not to have important events surprise us in this way
verdicts.note: Raw page, after the Aragorn / Pelennor Fields example: 'Kay seems determined not to have important events surprise us in this way; he arranges the story's kernels in a more tightly-knit fashion than does Tolkien, mainly through a much more frequent shifting of our attention from one character to another.' Note Randall hedges with 'seems determined'; the claim states it flatly.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the flat assertion that Kay keeps important events from surprising the reader — the note records that Randall hedges with "seems determined" while the claim states it flatly.

verdicts.trueWording: twenty-one separate focalizants in Tigana, and more than 150 separate focalizations
verdicts.note: Raw page, footnote 1: 'In addition to the non-focalized narrative, there are twenty-one separate focalizants in Tigana, and more than 150 separate focalizations. Devin is focalized through forty-one times, and Dianora twenty-seven times. There are twenty-one separate occasions of non-focalized narrative, excluding short passages with zero focalization within focalized sections.' All five figures match. The 21 non-focalized occasions EXCLUDE short zero-focalized passages inside focalized sections - carry that qualifier if the figure is re-used.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "twenty-one separate non-focalized passages" stated without scope — the note says the figure EXCLUDES short zero-focalized passages inside focalized sections and that the qualifier must be carried.

verdicts.trueWording: he is central to all the story kernels ... and the originator of the fabula
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'Returning to Brandin, he is central to all the story kernels of Tigana, and the originator of the fabula. Yet, Brandin is only focalized through at the very end of the battle ... By this point, the readers have had time to assimilate all the information given about the Sorcerer King and thus had the chance to form their own opinion about him before Kay reveals what Brandin thinks of himself. No more than a page long, Brandin's focalization is one of the most powerful sections of the story.' Kleander's wording is 'had the chance to form their own opinion', slightly weaker than 'has already formed a judgment'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "after the reader has already formed a judgment" — the note says Kleander's wording is "had the chance to form their own opinion", "slightly weaker" than the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: clearest example … can be seen in the prayers of the Asharites and the Jaddites
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. The page then prints the two prayer paragraphs consecutively (LoAR 251-252 and the Jaddite counterpart), and they are near-identical in frame ('They prayed for strength and mercy, for purity of heart and mortal body, for the fulfilment of Ashar’s starlit visions / Jad’s bright visions … to Paradise'). Kleander frames it as 'Rather than focusing on differences, Kay focuses on similarities.' She demonstrates the parallel rather than naming it 'structural repetition', but the mechanism is on the page verbatim.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "structural repetition" as Kleander's framing — the note says she demonstrates the parallel "rather than naming it 'structural repetition'".

verdicts.trueWording: GGK NOTE ... the source of my dissent from her reading
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact. Kay's signed note ('- GGK') disputes Webb's gender reading directly: his dissent 'lies in the degree to which the text tries to make clear that it is an anomaly and a dangerous one that a woman is reigning in Arbonne', against her reading of the Blaise/Rinette marriage as a traditional union of male and female principles; 'unusual and generous step' supports the rarity limb. Placement detail: the note is interpolated mid-essay, immediately after the passage it answers, not at the very end.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "appended" — the note says the GGK NOTE is interpolated mid-essay immediately after the passage it answers, "not at the very end".

verdicts.trueWording: what happened that night in a burning hamlet near Fezana became legendary
verdicts.note: Same raw page. The block quote Ordway sets off is the surgery passage: ben Yonannon, blind and mute, 'carved an opening in the skull of Diego Belmonte' and removed the bone fragment. Its first sentence ends 'became legendary' (quote verbatim), and the passage is explicitly retrospective/legend-framing ('In Al-Rassan, in Esperana, Ferrieres, Karch, Batiara - even, in time, in the far-off eastern homelands of the Asharites -'). Minor: the sentence opens with that place-list before reaching 'what happened that night', so 'opens' means the opening sentence, not the first words.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "opens 'what happened that night... became legendary'" — the note says the sentence opens with the place-list before reaching those words, so they are not the passage's first words.

verdicts.trueWording: only supernatural the societies believed; shown inside-out; setting renders beliefs true
verdicts.note: Cawsey's introduction (p.310): "the rest of Kay's works follow this general rule: they only contain elements of the supernatural that the original societies would have believed or at least half-believed"; "show the beliefs and assumptions of a time period from the inside-out"; "Kay says in the Tolkien lecture that the setting 'renders these beliefs as true.'" Two minor page qualifiers the claim drops but does not contradict: "or at least half-believed", and Ysabel (2007) is named as the exception. The quoted phrase is Kay's, from the Tolkien lecture, as reported in Cawsey's introduction. PDF fetched directly and text-extracted with pypdf.
